summary: A note from SRI-ARC on how the NIC Journal would use FTP for mail delivery and submission. SRI first planned to hide parameters in the username field of MLFL, but the Network Mail Meeting preferred changing FTP so that parameters are stated explicitly. It describes what the NIC wanted.

plainLanguage.summary: A library said how it wanted to receive and send messages through the file-sending program and agreed to change the rules to make that clean.

questions: how to use ftp for journal
subtitle: How the Network Information Center would use FTP commands for journal submission and delivery.

tldr.problem: The NIC Journal needed a way to accept mail submissions and deliver journal articles through the network. The authors initially wanted to hide parameters in the FTP username field.
tldr.mechanism: SRI-ARC proposes making FTP parameters explicit through dedicated sub-commands (TITLE, USER-READABLE-AUTHOR, PROCESS-READABLE-AUTHOR, ACKNOWLEDGMENT-DETAILS, ADDRESSEES-ARE, MAIL-CLASS, RECORD, and others) rather than encoding them in the username.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes what the NIC wanted from FTP and the consensus to make parameters explicit, leaving syntax details to the FTP Interest Group.

facts.label: New sub-commands
facts.value: TITLE, author fields, ACKNOWLEDGMENT-DETAILS, ADDRESSEES-ARE, MAIL-CLASS, RECORD, TEXT, FILE, and others

facts.label: Recipient identifier types
facts.value: NIC Ident, username@hostname, or name lookup

today: RFC 479 describes conceptual requirements without specifying final syntax. The NIC Journal system was eventually implemented but FTP was not the primary mechanism for modern email. SMTP and related protocols became the standard for mail submission and delivery.

sections.title: Journal Submission Meets FTP
sections.content:
The NIC maintained a shared journal where network users could submit and receive articles. The RFC proposes using FTP, specifically the MLFL (mail file) command, to support this. Initially, the authors planned to encode journal parameters (such as recipient IDs) inside the FTP username field, keeping the FTP protocol unchanged.

However, at the Network Mail Meeting, participants agreed it was better to modify FTP explicitly to accept parameters as real commands rather than hidden in usernames.
sections.plainLanguage: The NIC wanted to accept journal articles through the mail system. At first they planned to hide journal instructions in the username. But everyone agreed it was cleaner to add real commands.

sections.title: New FTP Sub-Commands
sections.content:
The proposal describes sub-commands that would support journal operations. TITLE and author fields (USER-READABLE-AUTHOR, PROCESS-READABLE-AUTHOR, FOR-ACKNOWLEDGMENT-AUTHOR) let the sender identify themselves. ACKNOWLEDGMENT-DETAILS controls when and how delivery notifications are sent. ADDRESSEES-ARE specifies recipients by NIC identity, host address, or name.

MAIL-CLASS indicates size (BULK or POSTCARD) and urgency (SPECIAL-DELIVERY or FIRST-CLASS). RECORD tells the server to journalize the mail and optionally assigns an identifier. PRESERVED-AT states where a copy is stored. TEXT or FILE sends the actual message or a pointer to it.
sections.plainLanguage: Each sub-command does one job: one says who wrote it, one says who gets it, one says how urgent it is, and so on. This is much clearer than hiding things in the username.

sections.title: The NIC's Unique Role
sections.content:
The RFC notes that the NIC acts as a forwarding agent for journal articles. When a user sends mail to the NIC, the NIC stores it, then sends copies to each listed recipient. From the sender's perspective, delivery to the NIC is just submission, not final delivery. This is why the FOR-ACKNOWLEDGMENT-AUTHOR field exists: the NIC will send a separate acknowledgment when the article reaches its final recipients.

Some sub-commands apply only at the NIC; others are general enough that other sites might adopt them later.
sections.plainLanguage: The NIC is not like a normal mail server. It receives articles, catalogs them, and then sends them to the real readers. So it needs a special kind of delivery confirmation.
